title: Gauge in pattern stitch vs stocking stitch
subtitle: Why textured stitches need their own swatch, not a stocking-stitch proxy.
excerpt: Cable, rib, and textured stitches pull the fabric in and change the stitch count per 10 cm. A stocking-stitch swatch is not a reliable substitute when the pattern body is a different stitch.
sourceNotes: Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), chapter on tension and fabric. Weldon's Practical Knitter pattern instructions, which specify tension in the pattern stitch for textured designs. Craft Yarn Council tension guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: The tension measured in the stitch used for the body of the piece, not in stocking stitch. Cables and ribs pull inward, producing a denser fabric with more stitches per 10 cm than a plain stocking-stitch swatch.

content.text: Stocking stitch is open. Cables and ribbing pull the fabric inward, which means the same yarn on the same needles will produce more stitches per 10 cm in a textured pattern than in plain stocking stitch. A stocking-stitch swatch is not a valid substitute for a

check when the body of the piece is cabled or heavily textured. The difference can be as large as four stitches per 10 cm on a dense Aran cable, which would change the finished width of a sweater by several centimetres. Difficulty: intermediate, because it requires working a larger swatch and understanding why the numbers differ.
Project yarn and the recommended needle size
A cable needle if the pattern includes cables
Swatching in the pattern stitch, step by step
Cast on enough stitches to complete at least two full repeats of the pattern stitch, plus a few plain stitches on each side to stop the edges from curling.
Work the pattern stitch for at least 15 cm. Cables need height to settle into their correct width.
Cast off and block exactly as you plan to block the finished piece.
Lay flat and pin two points 10 cm apart horizontally. Count the stitches within that distance, measuring in the pattern stitch itself, not in an adjacent plain column.
Compare your count to the pattern's stated tension. Adjust needle size and reswatch until they match.

Aran sweater patterns almost always state tension in the cable pattern and separately in stocking stitch. Ribbed sweater bodies carry their tension in the rib. Any pattern where the main body stitch is not plain stocking stitch should be swatched in that body stitch.

items.symptom: Swatch tension matches but finished fabric looks different
items.cause: Cables loosen slightly after blocking when worked over a larger area
items.fix: Wet-block the swatch fully and leave it to dry completely before measuring. A cable swatch measured damp will read wider than it will set.

items.symptom: Pattern states tension in stocking stitch but the body is all cables
items.cause: Some older patterns state a stocking-stitch tension even for textured pieces
items.fix: Work both swatches: one in stocking stitch to match the stated tension, and one in the cable repeat to understand the actual body width. Use both readings to plan the finished size.
